It's Monday, 7 a.m. Your alarm goes off. But it doesn't sound like your alarm.
You open your eyes. The ceiling is wrong. The bed is huge. And there's a tie hanging on the door.
You walk to the mirror. And your dad is staring back at you.
Oh no. Oh no, no, no.
Across the hall, someone screams. It's you. Well, your body. With your dad inside.
Why am I so short? Why does this room smell like socks?
In the kitchen, your mom takes a sip of coffee. And makes the worst face you have ever seen.
This is disgusting. How do you drink this every day?
Give me that. And why are my legs so short?
Somehow, overnight, everyone swapped. You got Dad's life. Dad got yours. Mom and your sister switched too.
So, what if you swapped lives with your parents for a week?
Okay, rules. It lasts exactly seven days. Next Monday at 7 a.m., everything goes back.
You have to live their life completely. Their job. Their school. Their bills. Their problems.
And nobody outside this house can know. If anyone finds out, the swap becomes permanent.
Permanent? I am not doing sixth grade math again.
Relax, Dad. How hard can school be?
He gives you a long look. With your own face.
Monday. And at first, being an adult feels amazing.
You want to drive Dad's car. Then you remember you're twelve inside. So you take the bus. In a tie.
At Dad's office, you get your own desk. Your own computer. Free coffee. Nobody tells you to sit up straight.
Morning. I need that report by three.
You have no idea what a report is. So you open Dad's computer, and you find two hundred and forty unread emails.
Meanwhile, at your school, your dad sits in your seat. His knees don't fit under the desk. Wait, they do. He's tiny now.
Okay, pop quiz. Fractions. Phones away.
A pop quiz? On a Monday? Who does that?
Your dad hasn't done fractions in twenty-five years. He gets four out of ten.
Monday night. You come home from work, and all you want to do is lie on the couch.
But there's a problem. Your kid has homework. And your kid is your dad.
Can you help me with this? It's about the water cycle.
At nine o'clock, you send him to bed. He complains. Loudly.
Not this week, buddy. Lights out.
You have never felt so powerful in your life.
Tuesday. Dad's phone buzzes. It's the bank.
And this is when you see it. Dad's account.
It looks like a lot of money. Way more than your allowance.
We're rich! Why didn't anyone tell me we're rich?
The car payment. The electricity. Internet. Phone. Insurance. Groceries.
You put it all on the kitchen table and do the math. On your fingers.
Wait. Where did the money go?
It's Tuesday. And almost all of Dad's paycheck is already gone.
And Mom? Mom is in your little sister's body. Which means Mom is in second grade.
At ten o'clock, the teacher says it's nap time. Everyone lies down on a little mat.
Nap time? You mean I'm allowed to sleep? In the middle of the day?
She sleeps for two hours. It's the best day of her adult life.
When she wakes up, she has glitter in her hair and a gold star on her hand. She doesn't know why. She doesn't care.
Wednesday, Mom sends you to the grocery store. With a list. And a budget.
You put chips in the cart. Then cookies. Then a pizza. Then three more pizzas.
At the checkout, the number keeps going up.
Your little sister. In Mom's body. With Mom's exact voice. And Mom's exact look.
That night, it's your turn to cook dinner. For four people. Every night. Forever. Well, for a week.
You make pasta. You forget the water. The smoke alarm goes off.
Dinner is cereal. Again. Nobody complains. Out loud.
Meanwhile, at school, it's gym class. Dodgeball.
Your dad thinks he's still good at sports. He is not. He's twelve now, and his arms are noodles.
The first ball hits him in the face. The second one too.
Are you okay? You look like you've seen a ghost.
I have seen my own childhood. And it hurts.
Back at the office, you have a video meeting with eleven people. You forget to turn off your camera.
Everyone watches you eat cereal out of the box for six minutes.
And here's the part that's actually real.
The US government once added up what it costs to raise one kid. Food, clothes, a bedroom, school, doctors. From birth until age seventeen.
The answer? About two hundred thirty-three thousand dollars. For one kid.
And that was years ago. Today, it's even more.
Two hundred thirty-three thousand. That's a house in a lot of places. And your parents are paying it. For you.
Huh. Maybe I should stop asking for new sneakers.
Thursday. You still haven't written the report.
Where's the report? It was due Monday.
You don't. You realize that, too late.
That evening, there's a parent-teacher meeting. About your son. Who is your dad.
Your son is having a hard time. Four out of ten on fractions. And he keeps calling me "ma'am."
I'll talk to him. He's a good kid. He just needs more screen time.
In the hallway, your dad is waiting. In your body. With his arms crossed.
Meanwhile, Dad has a very different problem. At recess, he tried to talk to the other kids about mortgages.
Now nobody wants to sit with him at lunch.
They said I talk like a dad. I am a dad!
And at home? Mom is in your sister's body. Her feet don't reach the pedals. She can't drive.
And your sister is in Mom's body. She has the credit card.
Just a pony. A small one.
And for the first time, you don't think "we're rich." You think, "That's it? For a whole week of this?"
You sit down with the bills again. This time, you do it right. With a calculator.
Rent first. Then food. Then the car, the lights, the phone. Then everything else.
And there's a little bit left. Not a lot. But enough.
That night, everyone ends up in the kitchen. Nobody can sleep.
I forgot how hard school is. Homework, tests, nobody listens to you.
And I didn't know how hard your job is. Or how fast the money goes.
I didn't know how small this kitchen looks from down here.
And I didn't know a pony costs this much to feed.
For a moment, it's quiet. And then everyone laughs. Even the pony, probably.
Saturday, you all go to the park. You in Dad's body. Dad in yours. Pushing each other on the swings.
It's weird. But it's the best day of the week.
At five o'clock, a truck stops in front of the house. Somebody forgot to cancel the second pony.
Sunday, you make a plan. Seven a.m. tomorrow, everyone in the kitchen. Hands together. Count to three.
And after this, you are doing your own fractions.
Deal. And you're writing your own report.
So on Sunday afternoon, you finally write the report. Dad sits next to you and explains every word.
And then you help him with fractions. You draw a pizza. You cut it into eight pieces.
Oh. Oh! That's what three eighths means?
You've been an adult for twenty-five years and you didn't know that?
I knew it. I just forgot it. Like you'll forget it. Trust me.
Monday. 6:59. Everyone is ready. The clock ticks.
Seven a.m. You close your eyes. You count to three.
You open your eyes. You look down.
And you're still in Dad's body.
Then the front door opens. It's your boss.
Good morning. I just came by to say... wait. Why is everyone holding hands?
Somebody outside the house is about to find out.
And if anyone finds out, the swap becomes permanent.
